title: BrightScale - Throughput tuning technical deep dive
summary: Deep technical discussion about tuning Redwood runtime for BrightScale's mixed workload (short chat + long generations). Covered continuous batching parameters, scheduler knobs (latency SLO vs throughput tradeoffs), max_num_seqs tuning, token limits, KV cache warmup, quantization impact, and VPC deployment considerations. Agreed to run a 72-hour benchmark and share kernel-level logs.
next_steps: Redwood: run 72-hour continuous batching benchmark on BrightScale sample workload and share results (Evan)
BrightScale: provide 1 week of anonymized traces and representative prompt set (Carlos)
Schedule follow-up to review benchmark and SLO tuning (calendar invite from Evan)
action_items: Evan: spin up benchmark harness + baseline config and share runbook by 2026-12-23
Sana: include scheduler and kernel-level tracing flags and include example traces by 2026-12-23
Carlos: upload 10k sample prompts + traffic histogram to shared S3 by 2026-12-22
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-21 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Evan, Sana, Liam, Maya (Redwood); Carlos, Priya, Derek, Hannah (BrightScale)

[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — throughput tuning, continuous batching, and then an architectural Q&A on VPC/on-prem alignment. Carlos, do you want to kick off with current pain points?

[00:17] Carlos: Yeah, thanks. We're seeing this weird pattern where short chat requests are fine but when workers hit long generations our p99 jumps up 3x, and overall cost is spiky. We're running a mixed workloads on a dedicated pool, NVLink gen 4, gpus, uh — with micro-batching at app level.

[00:35] Sana: ok, couple of quick clarifying q's — what's your current batching mode? Are you using Redwood continuous batching or manual batching in front?

[00:43] Priya: We have app-side batching mostly, like groups of 8, and then we set server-side max_num_seqs to 16. We didn't fully trust automatic continuous batching.

[00:57] Sana: got it. So two levers: continuous batching in the runtime which will combine sequences across requests for better GPU utilization, and scheduler knobs — max_num_seqs, target_latency, and the per-instance token cap.

[01:15] Derek: When you say token cap, is that per-request or global per-gpu? Because we throttle at the container layer currently and that seems to cause head-of-line blocking.

[01:25] Liam: in Redwood the token limits are enforced at the runtime scheduling layer — you can set max_tokens_per_batch and also max_num_seqs. If app-level throttling pre-buffers, it can either help or hurt depending on distribution.

[01:40] Hannah: can you explain head-of-line blocking again in plain terms?

[01:43] Sana: sure — imagine a long generation sitting at the head of the scheduler queue; if the scheduler prioritizes FIFO, short requests behind it wait. Continuous batching with dynamic prioritization can form batches that exclude the long run or limit its impact by slicing tokens and interleaving. But there are tradeoffs in kernel warmup and kv cache thrashing.

[02:05] Carlos: kv cache thrashing — we've noticed latency spikes when different conversations with long context keep populating the KV cache. Is that expected?

[02:12] Sana: yes, especially with long contexts and multiple users; the KV cache is per-sequence and per-model. If you have high variance in seq lengths, the cache can bounce and memory pressure causes eviction; that leads to re-computation and higher tail latency. Strategies: prefix caching for common prompts, eviction policies tuned to recency + size, and in some cases quantized KV storage which reduces memory but adds small compute overhead.

[02:42] Priya: We can't lose user context; eviction policies worry us from a correctness perspective. Any guidance on safe settings?

[02:50] Sana: set max_num_seqs to cover your median concurrent seqs and then use a hot-prefix cache for top N frequent flows. Also ensure the scheduler's sequence bucketing groups similar seq lengths. We can share a script to analyze your traces to recommend max_num_seqs and token caps.

[03:10] Evan: quick interjection — on quantization: 4-bit quantization reduces memory footprint allowing more seqs per GPU but can increase per-token compute (small) and sometimes impacts generation quality. For throughput wins on NVLink setups, it's often net-positive.

[03:26] Carlos: are there specific kernel-level flags we should flip? Our infra team wants CLI-level guidance.

[03:31] Sana: yes — two main flags: enable_continuous_batching=true and scheduler_mode=latency_aware (or throughput_opt for batch-heavy). Also set kernel_tracing=1 for benchmark runs so we can capture queuing times, kernel exec, and kv cache metrics. We'll include example configs.

[03:50] Derek: how does scheduler_mode=latency_aware differ? Does it preempt long jobs?

[03:56] Sana: it's a weighted priority queue. Latency_aware scores requests by expected remaining tokens and recent latency; it will preferentially form small batches for short requests and still subsume long ones when beneficial. Throughput_opt will prefer full batches even if p99 tolerances stretch.

[04:18] Priya: our SLO is 200ms p95 for chat, and 2s p95 for longer summarizations. How do we configure this?

[04:25] Liam: you'd set per-route SLOs in the routing layer and map them to scheduler profiles. Route 'chat' -> scheduler_profile: latency_aware with max_num_seqs 8 and token_cap 256; route 'long' -> throughput_opt with max_num_seqs 32 and token_cap 2048. The runtime supports per-route overrides.

[04:50] Carlos: ok interesting — what's a safe starting point for max_num_seqs for our fleet? We're at median concurrency of ~60 sequences across 6 nodes.

[04:59] Sana: rule of thumb: max_num_seqs per worker = ceil(median_concurrency / active_workers) * 1.25. So with 6 nodes, ~60/6=10 -> start with 12-16 and run the benchmark. But monitor queueing and kv memory.

[05:20] Hannah: about the benchmark — what should it look like? We want to reproduce mixed traffic.

[05:25] Evan: We'll run a 72-hour continuous workload that mimics your traffic histogram: 70% short chat (mean 40 tokens), 25% mid (200 tokens), 5% long (1500 tokens). We'll sweep max_num_seqs at 8, 16, 32 and quantization at 8-bit and 4-bit to measure cost/latency tradeoffs.

[05:46] Priya: any risk of model quality regressions with 4-bit on our LLaMA-derivative?

[05:51] Sana: small risk; we recommend eval hooks in the benchmark — run ngrams and a small eval prompt set to watch for regressions. We'll attach Redwood Optimize suggestions if we detect drift.

[06:05] Carlos: about VPC/on-prem — we plan to move this to a private deployment in Q1. How does that affect continuous batching and kernel choices?

[06:13] Liam: the runtime is identical, but kernel selection may vary by driver versions and the GPU microcode. On-prem you might have different NCCL/driver stacks; we provide a compatibility matrix. Continuous batching still works — it's purely runtime-level. However, networked KV cache (if you use remote KV for huge contexts) adds latency; prefer local NVMe-backed cache for low tail latency.

[06:38] Derek: NVMe-backed — do you have recommended sizing?

[06:41] Sana: size about 2-3x your active context working set. For BrightScale's traffic, initial estimate is 1TB per node if you keep long histories; but with prefixing and TTL it's less. We'll analyze once we get traces.

[06:54] Hannah: ok. Let's talk about scheduler knobs that are often overlooked.

[06:58] Evan: set target_fill_time_ms — that's the window the scheduler waits to form a batch. Lower values reduce latency but reduce GPU efficiency. Typical starting values: chat route 10-20ms, throughput route 50-100ms. Also set max_batch_age_ms to prevent starvation.

[07:20] Priya: those numbers seem quite low — do GPUs benefit from such small windows?

[07:25] Sana: when you have high request rates with many short requests, even 10-20ms can significantly increase tokens/sec because the scheduler aggregates across many sequences. But it's workload dependent; that's why we'll run the sweep.

[07:40] Carlos: can we do adaptive target_fill_time that changes during peak hours?

[07:44] Liam: yes, the orchestration layer supports dynamic profiles based on traffic tiers — we can tie it to auto-scaling signals. For example, during peak you bias towards throughput_opt and increase target_fill_time.

[07:58] Derek: what about preemption? If a long generation is in progress, can we pause it to schedule short latency requests?

[08:04] Sana: not pause mid-kernel; but you can slice long generations into smaller token windows (server-side chunking) and the scheduler can interleave. That requires model support for incremental generation state; our runtime supports checkpointing KV per-slice.

[08:21] Carlos: sounds complex. Is there an easy win we can try quickly?

[08:24] Evan: enable continuous batching with scheduler_mode=latency_aware and reduce max_num_seqs slightly for chat routes. Also enable kernel tracing and run for 24 hours to see immediate gains.

[08:36] Priya: ok. For the benchmark logs — what format do you need?

[08:40] Sana: flamegraph-style traces are great plus per-token latency CSVs. We also need queuing time, exec time, kv hits/misses, and memory pressure events. We'll provide a sample schema.

[08:54] Hannah: on data privacy — the traces will have user content; we need to ensure redaction.

[08:58] Evan: understood. Provide anonymized prompts; we can accept hashed prompts and token histograms. For private deployment you'll keep control of keys; Redwood receives only metrics.

[09:10] Derek: you mentioned kernel selection and quantization — could different GPU families behave differently? We're testing both A100 and H100.

[09:17] Sana: yes H100s have different tensor core behavior; quantization to 4-bit often shows better throughput on H100 but may require different kernel params. We'll include per-GPU recommended kernel flags in the runbook.

[09:31] Priya: any known issues with mixed precision and KV cache?

[09:35] Liam: mixed precision can affect memory layout; ensure the KV cache alignment matches kernel expectations; misalignment can cause small perf regressions. Our codepath handles alignment but older driver combos can be funky — we'll validate in the benchmark.

[09:49] Carlos: if continuous batching increases throughput but hurts p95 a bit, how do we present that to stakeholders?

[09:55] Evan: show cost per token and p95/p99 tradeoffs. Often a small p95 increase is acceptable given 30-50% cost reductions. We'll produce a cost/latency Pareto chart from the benchmark.

[10:10] Priya: ok. Let's dig into a concrete config example — can you walk through an example JSON for two routes?

[10:15] Sana: sure — (reads) route: chat -> scheduler_profile: latency_aware, max_num_seqs: 12, target_fill_time_ms: 15, token_cap: 256; route: summarization -> scheduler_profile: throughput_opt, max_num_seqs: 32, target_fill_time_ms: 60, token_cap: 2048. We'll paste this in the follow-up notes.

[10:36] Derek: one more question on cache warmup: if we warm pre-populate KV for known flows, does it change batch formation?

[10:43] Sana: it can. Warm prefixes reduce cold misses and reduce generation time, but if too many warm contexts exist they increase memory pressure. Use targeted warm-up for top N flows.

[10:54] Carlos: ok, I'm convinced. What's the likely delta if we go from app-level batching to Redwood continuous batching?

[10:59] Evan: customers typically see 1.5x-3x throughput improvement for short-heavy workloads. For mixed workloads, 1.3x-2x depending on variance and kernel tuning.

[11:12] Priya: that's promising. Let's confirm deliverables and timeline.

[11:16] Evan: deliverables: benchmark harness + runbook (by 12/23), sample config + tracing flags (12/23), BrightScale traces upload (12/22). We'll wrap with a 1-hour review after the benchmark (week of 12/27).

[11:30] Carlos: cool. Any blockers on your side?

[11:33] Sana: none; just access to traces and a target endpoint. Also confirm GPU family and driver versions.

[11:40] Hannah: we'll share infra details after the call. Thanks everyone.

[11:45] Evan: thanks all — we'll follow up with the runbook and calendar invite.

End of transcript.
